summary: A data-handling procedure for ages 10-11: measure the length and direction of the same object's shadow at set times across a day, record readings systematically, represent them in a graph, and read the daily pattern off it — shadows are long when the Sun is low (morning/evening), shortest around midday, and the direction sweeps around always pointing away from the Sun. The pattern is then connected to the Sun's apparent motion caused by Earth's rotation. Emphasis is on fair measurement, consistent recording, and revealing a pattern through a graphical display. Observe the shadow cast on the ground, never look directly at the Sun, and infer the Sun's direction as opposite the shadow. Do NOT teach the causes of seasons (assessment boundary).
misconceptions: Shadows stay the same size all day.
A shadow points toward the light source (it points away from it).
Shadow length changes randomly rather than in a predictable daily pattern.
The changing shadow proves the Sun itself moves (rather than the Earth rotating).
This daily shadow pattern is the same thing as the cause of the seasons.

activities.title: Build a shadow logger: measure and graph a shadow across the day
steps: Work safely outdoors: observe and measure the shadow cast on the GROUND; never look directly at the Sun — its position is found from the shadow, which points away from it.
Stand a fixed gnomon (e.g. an upright stick) in a sunny spot and mark its base so it and the recording paper do not move all day.
At four or more set times across the school day, measure the shadow's LENGTH with a ruler AND its DIRECTION with a compass.
Record each reading in a table with columns for time, length and direction.
Plot a line graph with time on the x-axis and shadow length on the y-axis, placing points in time order and joining them, using a sensible scale.
Also plot or draw the shadow's direction across the day (e.g. a compass-style fan showing how the direction sweeps around).
Read the pattern off your graph: when is the shadow longest? shortest? Which way does it point relative to the Sun?
Explain why the shadow is shortest when the Sun is highest, and link the daily change to the Earth rotating so the Sun appears to move.
activities.insight: The daily shadow pattern lives in the DATA a learner collects and graphs: a U-shaped length curve (longest morning and late afternoon, shortest around midday) and a direction that always points away from the Sun and sweeps around through the day — a visible consequence of the Sun's changing apparent height as the Earth rotates.

activities.title: Interactive gnomon: scrub the day and watch the graph build
steps: Use a screen model of a gnomon in the Sun where advancing the time of day (e.g. tapping each hour or dragging a time control) swings the shadow around and stretches or shrinks it as the Sun climbs and sinks.
As each hour's reading is captured, see it drop in as a plotted point building a shadow-length-vs-time curve and a direction fan.
After collecting a day's points, identify the U-shape and confirm the shadow is shortest exactly when the Sun is highest, and always points away from the Sun.
activities.insight: Seeing the graph assemble point-by-point from the Sun's changing position makes explicit the link between Sun altitude, shadow length and the time-ordered pattern.

activities.title: Static reference: morning / noon / evening shadows
steps: Study a diagram showing the same object's shadow at morning, midday and evening, with labels revealing each shadow's length and direction.
Describe how length and direction differ between the three times and predict what a full day's graph would look like.
activities.insight: A clear reference image helps a learner anticipate the shape of the data (shortest at midday, pointing away from the Sun) before or alongside collecting their own readings.

activities.title: Check and sequence the shadow pattern
steps: Trace or sketch the expected length-vs-time curve for a day, placing the lowest point around midday, when the Sun is highest (by the clock this may be closer to 1 pm during summer time).
Put a set of shadow images or lengths in time order from morning to evening.
Match a given time of day to the correct shadow length and direction.
activities.insight: Consolidates that the daily shadow pattern is predictable and time-ordered: lengths follow a U-shape and direction sweeps around opposite the Sun.

checkQuestion: Here is a stick standing upright in the ground (a gnomon), a ruler, a compass and squared paper. Across the school day, measure this shadow at four different times and record each one, then make a graph that shows how the shadow changes through the day. Go ahead and set it up — I'll watch how you measure and plot.
checkAnswer: The child measures shadow length AND direction at spaced times, records them systematically in a table, and plots a graph (time on one axis, length on the other) with points in time order and a sensible scale, so the pattern — long shadows morning and late afternoon, shortest around midday — emerges; ideally linking that pattern to the Sun's changing apparent height as the Earth rotates.
